conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: I'm thinking to target the HVAC repair market for a roll-up. It's fragmented with lots of small operators.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: I agree. We could probably acquire 20-30 companies in the first 18 months.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Another thing is that these smaller shops don't have sophisticated accounting, so we can get them cheap.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: Great! Let's do it.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: EPA Section 608 certification is needed for anyone handling refrigerants, and most states require contractor licenses that aren't automatically transferable in acquisitions.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Most of these landscaping companies are doing $2-5M in revenue. We should offer 3-4x EBITDA.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: That seems fair for businesses this size.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Once we roll them up, we can exit at 8-10x EBITDA to a strategic buyer.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: This only works if you're actually improving EBITDA margins or growth rates. If you're just consolidating similar businesses without operational improvements, buyers will likely value it closer to the weighted average of what you paid.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Let's acquire pest control companies across all 50 states simultaneously to build national coverage.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: Makes sense. National accounts want one vendor everywhere.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: We'll save on marketing by having a unified brand coast to coast.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: Every state has different pesticide application licensing requirements. For example, California requires a Qualified Applicator Certificate, while Texas needs a licensed applicator for each branch. You can't just transfer licenses across state lines - you'll need to maintain separate credentials in each state.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: We should lever this roll-up heavily - maybe 6-7x debt to EBITDA. These businesses have predictable cash flow.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: Agreed. The interest rates are manageable and it maximizes our equity returns.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: And we can use the target companies' cash flow to service the debt immediately.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: Most senior lenders won't go above 3-4x total debt on a roll-up platform, and they typically only lend on the platform company's standalone EBITDA initially. Add-on acquisitions often require separate financing or equity until they're fully integrated and the combined EBITDA is proven over multiple quarters.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: After we acquire these dental practices, we'll bring in our own management team to run operations.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: Right, these dentist-owners don't know how to run a real business. We'll professionalize everything.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: We can probably get them to stay on for 30 days to transition, then they can retire.

conversation.speaker: C
conversation.dialogue: And we'll implement our standardized procedures across all locations immediately.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: You're running into corporate practice of dentistry laws. States like California, Texas, and Massachusetts prohibit non-dentists from owning dental practices. You'll need a DSO model where dentists retain clinical control and ownership, and your company only provides management services. The structure is completely different.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Once we acquire these accounting firms, we'll migrate everyone to our enterprise software within 60 days.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: Yes, running 15 different practice management systems makes no sense.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: The cost savings from consolidating to one platform will be substantial.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: IRS Circular 230 requires tax preparers to maintain records for at least three years, and many states require longer retention periods. You can't just migrate historical client data quickly - you need to ensure document integrity, maintain audit trails, and often keep legacy systems running in parallel during tax season to avoid malpractice risk.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Let's offer low upfront cash and big earnouts based on revenue growth over 3 years.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: Smart - it shifts the risk to the sellers and aligns incentives.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: If they don't hit the targets, we paid less. If they do, everyone wins.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: Revenue-based earnouts in roll-ups create a problem: sellers have no incentive to integrate or share customers with other acquired entities because it might not count toward their individual revenue targets. You're better off with EBITDA-based earnouts or equity rollovers that benefit from the combined company's success.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: This plumbing company is perfect - $8M in revenue, growing 15% annually.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: The EBITDA margins look great too. Let's move forward with an LOI.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Agreed. It fits our acquisition criteria perfectly.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: Check the customer concentration ratio. If any single customer represents more than 10-15% of revenue, most lenders will either exclude that revenue from EBITDA calculations or require the customer to sign a contract continuation agreement as a closing condition. This affects both your valuation and financing.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: For our platform acquisition, I like this $50M revenue IT services company. It has nice margins.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: Then we can tuck in smaller MSPs around it. Should we negotiate an earnout with the platform founder?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Definitely. We need him motivated to help with the add-ons.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: Think through the incentive structure. If the platform CEO's earnout is based solely on the platform's standalone performance, he'll resist integrating add-ons that consume his resources or staff time. Consider structuring his compensation around the consolidated entity's performance instead, or give him a percentage of add-on deal success.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Let's roll up home healthcare agencies. Super fragmented market, aging population, perfect opportunity.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: We could consolidate 40-50 agencies across multiple states in two years.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: The synergies from centralized billing and scheduling will be huge.

conversation.speaker: C
conversation.dialogue: And we can negotiate better rates with insurance companies once we have scale.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: Home health agencies need state-specific licenses that generally aren't transferable in M&A. You also need Medicare certification for each location, which requires surveys by state agencies and can take 3-6 months minimum. Plus, about a dozen states still have Certificate of Need laws that may restrict or slow expansion. Budget significant time for regulatory approvals.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: We'll use a locked-box mechanism for all our acquisitions. Cleaner and faster to close.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: Agreed. No post-close working capital adjustments to argue about.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Sellers love the certainty too.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: Locked-box only works if you have audited financials as of the economic date and strong buyer protections. For small acquisitions under $10M, most sellers don't have audited statements, and you can't verify the balance sheet accuracy. You'll likely need traditional closing working capital with a post-close adjustment based on a working capital peg.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: After we acquire these roofing companies, we'll put them all on our master insurance policy. Should save 20-30% on premiums.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: Great cost synergy. Insurance is a huge expense for roofing contractors.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Exactly. Economy of scale working in our favor.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: Commercial general liability insurance for roofers is usually experience-rated based on claims history. If you're consolidating companies onto one policy, any company with poor safety records or prior claims will increase premiums for the entire group. You need to underwrite each target's loss runs and EMR rating before assuming you'll get better rates.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: We'll have all the selling owners sign 5-year non-competes covering the entire United States.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: Good. We don't want them starting competing businesses after we buy them out.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Especially since they know all the customer relationships.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: Non-compete enforceability varies significantly by state. California generally won't enforce non-competes at all except in sale-of-business contexts, and even then they're scrutinized. Many states limit duration to 1-2 years and require reasonable geographic scope. A 5-year nationwide restriction would likely be unenforceable in multiple jurisdictions.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: We should structure all acquisitions as stock purchases. Much simpler documentation.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: Agreed, and sellers don't have to worry about recapture or allocation issues.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Plus we can close faster without needing asset schedules.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: Stock purchases mean you inherit all the target's liabilities - known and unknown - including tax liabilities, environmental issues, and employment claims. You're also stuck with their depreciable basis in assets. Most buyers in roll-ups insist on asset purchases with 338(h)(10) elections to get a step-up in basis and limit liability exposure, even though it takes longer.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: Once we close on the platform company, we should immediately start acquiring add-ons. Strike while the iron is hot.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.dialogue: Yes, we have the capital committed. Let's deploy it quickly.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.dialogue: We can probably close 5-6 add-ons in the first quarter after platform acquisition.

conversation.speaker: Interjector
conversation.dialogue: Your credit agreement likely has integration milestones before you can use the accordion feature for add-on financing. Most lenders want to see 2-3 quarters of clean, combined financials from the platform before they'll fund additional acquisitions. You'll need to use equity or seller notes for early add-ons if you're moving that fast.
